heterogeneous

/het-er-uh-JEE-nee-us/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Heterogeneous means varied in character; made up of dissimilar parts or many different kinds of things.

The night market's food stalls were gloriously heterogeneous, offering Ethiopian stews, Korean dumplings, Texas barbecue, and Sicilian pastries side by side.

Example

Professor Lin's robotics team was strikingly heterogeneous: a poetry major who wrote the manuals, a former electrician, a high school intern, and a retired air traffic controller. Their mismatched backgrounds turned out to be the team's greatest strength.

The team is built from members with very different backgrounds and skills, and a group made up of such dissimilar parts is exactly what heterogeneous describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

varied: Varied says only that many different types or forms are present. Heterogeneous is the stronger, more technical word: it stresses that the parts of one whole are genuinely dissimilar, and it is the term science and statistics reach for when describing such a mixture.

assorted: Assorted describes different sorts gathered on purpose into one set, the way a box of assorted chocolates is filled by design. Heterogeneous simply reports that a whole is made of dissimilar parts, whether anyone chose them or they merely ended up together.

diverse: Diverse celebrates the presence of many different kinds, and it often carries approval, as in praise for a diverse team. Heterogeneous is the neutral, descriptive cousin: it states that the parts of something are unalike without applauding or criticizing the mixture.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

uniform: the same throughout, without variation

homogeneous: made up of parts that are all the same kind

Where it sits · how unalike the parts are

mixed → heterogeneous → motley

mixed vs. heterogeneous: A mixed group simply contains more than one kind of member, while a heterogeneous group is built from noticeably different, dissimilar kinds of parts.

motley vs. heterogeneous: A heterogeneous collection is genuinely varied but can still fit together, while a motley one looks thrown together with no order at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — hetero-: different, other (from Greek heteros)

Root — gen: from Greek genos, kind, type, or birth

Suffix — -eous: adjective-forming ending, 'having the quality of'

Put it together: Heterogeneous assembles neatly from its Greek pieces: hetero-, 'different or other,' plus the root genos, 'kind or type,' plus the adjective ending -eous. Something heterogeneous is literally 'of different kinds,' the mirror opposite of homogeneous, 'of the same kind.'

Use the root in a new word: generation: Three generations of the family run the bakery together, and generation grows from the same Greek root, genos, meaning 'kind' or 'birth,' that hides inside heterogeneous.

Word Choice

formal, often technical

Heterogeneous is common in scientific and academic writing, as in 'a heterogeneous mixture' in chemistry or 'a heterogeneous population' in social science. Its direct opposite is homogeneous, and mixing up the two is a classic test-day trap, so read the middle syllables carefully.
